articles.title: Great Nicobar Island project: Final Calcutta High Court hearing deferred as Centre seeks to file affidavit, objections
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & High-Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: 1. Core Context & Background: Centre argues that the FRA is not implemented in the A&NI, objects to some petitions claiming that they should be heard by the NGT or SC; next hearing posted for January 13, 2027; court to hear Attorney General of India on January 22

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The Calcutta High Court’s final hearing in a batch of petitions alleging forest rights violations in diverting forest land for the Union government’s ₹92,000 crore Great Nicobar Island (GNI) project was deferred again on Wednesday (November 25, 2026), after the Centre sought time to file another affidavit and some documents on the question of tribal rights. The Centre argued that the Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006, is not implemented in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (A&NI), which the petitioners rebutted by noting that the Islands administration has already issued a certificate claiming that FRA rights have been settled, which is what is being challenged. The High Court Bench, led by Chief Justice Ravindra Vithalrao Ghuge, has now posted the hearing for the batch of petitions on January 13, 2027, when the court is also expected to begin hearing a petition that specifically challenged the A&NI administration’s orders claiming that all provisions of the FRA had been complied with in diverting 121 sq.km. for the GNI project. This comes after the Centre told the Supreme Court in October this year that it would be best if the “High Court is requested to consider and decide all such cases at the earliest”. On Wednesday, when the Calcutta High Court was about to start the final hearing in these petitions as per the orders of the Supreme Court, Additional Solicitor General (ASG) of India Vikramjit Banerjee submitted that the Centre wished to once again raise preliminary objections on the maintainability of some of the petitions. Further, on the question of tribal rights, the ASG said the Centre wished to submit one more affidavit with some additional documents. Attorney General for India, R. Venkatramani, also appeared before the High Court on Wednesday. Profile: The Great Nicobar project | Between the sea and the state The Centre’s lawyers argued that on the question of the FRA, the law that is alleged to have been violated, it has been the historical stand of the Union government, across administrations, that the FRA need not be pursued in A&NI because the Protection of Aboriginal Tribes Regulations, 1956, was already operational there. In response, the petitioner’s counsel pointed out that the A&NI administration had explicitly issued a certificate saying that the rights of local tribespeople had been settled under the FRA and that this certificate is what has been challenged. Further, the Centre submitted that it would like to continue arguing on the maintainability of two more petitions tagged as part of the same issue, noting that these two petitions dealt with matters that should be brought either before the National Green Tribunal or the Supreme Court.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: The petitioner’s counsel objected to this and clarified that these two petitions specifically deal with orders that reduce the buffer zones for two specific National Parks on Great Nicobar Island.

🚀 Science, Tech & Environment Paragraph #26 of 30 (25 NOV)

📰 Great Nicobar Island project: Final Calcutta High Court hearing deferred as Centre seeks to file affidavit, objections

📌 Published: 25 Nov 2026, 11:44:58 PM
🎙️ Desi Hinglish Voice Educator • 🚂 Live Train Line Highlight & Screen Lock

1. Core Context & Background: Centre argues that the FRA is not implemented in the A&NI, objects to some petitions claiming that they should be heard by the NGT or SC; next hearing posted for January 13, 2027; court to hear Attorney General of India on January 22

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The Calcutta High Court’s final hearing in a batch of petitions alleging forest rights violations in diverting forest land for the Union government’s ₹92,000 crore Great Nicobar Island (GNI) project was deferred again on Wednesday (November 25, 2026), after the Centre sought time to file another affidavit and some documents on the question of tribal rights. The Centre argued that the Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006, is not implemented in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (A&NI), which the petitioners rebutted by noting that the Islands administration has already issued a certificate claiming that FRA rights have been settled, which is what is being challenged. The High Court Bench, led by Chief Justice Ravindra Vithalrao Ghuge, has now posted the hearing for the batch of petitions on January 13, 2027, when the court is also expected to begin hearing a petition that specifically challenged the A&NI administration’s orders claiming that all provisions of the FRA had been complied with in diverting 121 sq.km. for the GNI project. This comes after the Centre told the Supreme Court in October this year that it would be best if the “High Court is requested to consider and decide all such cases at the earliest”. On Wednesday, when the Calcutta High Court was about to start the final hearing in these petitions as per the orders of the Supreme Court, Additional Solicitor General (ASG) of India Vikramjit Banerjee submitted that the Centre wished to once again raise preliminary objections on the maintainability of some of the petitions. Further, on the question of tribal rights, the ASG said the Centre wished to submit one more affidavit with some additional documents. Attorney General for India, R. Venkatramani, also appeared before the High Court on Wednesday. Profile: The Great Nicobar project | Between the sea and the state The Centre’s lawyers argued that on the question of the FRA, the law that is alleged to have been violated, it has been the historical stand of the Union government, across administrations, that the FRA need not be pursued in A&NI because the Protection of Aboriginal Tribes Regulations, 1956, was already operational there. In response, the petitioner’s counsel pointed out that the A&NI administration had explicitly issued a certificate saying that the rights of local tribespeople had been settled under the FRA and that this certificate is what has been challenged. Further, the Centre submitted that it would like to continue arguing on the maintainability of two more petitions tagged as part of the same issue, noting that these two petitions dealt with matters that should be brought either before the National Green Tribunal or the Supreme Court.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: The petitioner’s counsel objected to this and clarified that these two petitions specifically deal with orders that reduce the buffer zones for two specific National Parks on Great Nicobar Island.

क्रियान्वयन / ज़मीनी स्तर पर लागू करना — किसी योजना या फैसले को असलियत में पूरा करना।
✓ Syn: Execution, Enforcement, Fulfillment  |  ✖ Ant: Abandonment, Neglect, Cancellation
Maintainability (Noun)
महत्वपूर्ण विश्लेषणात्मक शब्द — इस लेख में 'Maintainability' मुख्य प्रभाव और नीतिगत स्थिति को स्पष्ट करता है।
✓ Syn: Significant, Substantial, Strategic  |  ✖ Ant: Insignificant, Negligible, Trivial
Administration (Noun)
महत्वपूर्ण विश्लेषणात्मक शब्द — इस लेख में 'Administration' मुख्य प्रभाव और नीतिगत स्थिति को स्पष्ट करता है।
✓ Syn: Significant, Substantial, Strategic  |  ✖ Ant: Insignificant, Negligible, Trivial
Operational (Adjective)
महत्वपूर्ण विश्लेषणात्मक शब्द — इस लेख में 'Operational' मुख्य प्रभाव और नीतिगत स्थिति को स्पष्ट करता है।
✓ Syn: Comprehensive, Influential, Decisive  |  ✖ Ant: Superficial, Ineffective, Fragile

A. Centre argues that the FRA is not implemented in the A&NI, objects to some petitions claiming that they should be heard by the NGT or SC; next...
B. Contrary to the passage, the issue of 'Great Nicobar Island project: Final Calcutta Hig' requires zero institutional or regulatory intervention at any level.

articles.title: India’s satellite supply chain ‘highly dependent on imports’, says space body
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & High-Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: 1. Core Context & Background: India’s space economy is currently valued at nearly $9 billion and is set to grow to $40-45 billion in less than a decade

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: India’s satellite supply chain is “highly dependent” on imports for critical components and the private sector’s contribution is limited to “structural assemblies” and “propulsion components” largely supplied by established public sector firms and vintage private firms, said a report by IN-SPACe, India’s regulatory-cum-promotional body for the private space sector. While pointing out the potential of India’s private space companies, the autonomous body under the Department of Space underlined the challenges ahead. Science Minister Jitendra Singh earlier this week said that India’s space economy is currently valued at nearly $9 billion and is set to increase to $40-45 billion in less than a decade, with the private sector set to grow from a a few startups “to nearly 400-500 companies in just a few years”. The Supply Chain Landscape of Satellite Manufacturing in India report, which was made public on Wednesday, says that nearly 60% of satellite costs were attributed to electronic, electrical and electromechanical components, and specialised materials, many of which are imported. India also has limited testing and certification facilities, which weakened prospects for acceptance in global markets. Many companies largely operated on a “project-based manufacturing model”, which disincentivised long-term investment in automation and production capacity, the report noted. Critical components often took a long time to procure – frequently 12-16 months – which led to project delays and hobbled responsiveness to market opportunities. There was also a shortage of trained and skilled personnel in satellite systems engineering, quality assurance, testing and qualification, besides limited private-sector research and development and technology transfer. The report was prepared by Brijesh Kumar Sol and Yudhishthir J. of IN-SPACe and “approved” by Pawan Goenka, IN-SPACe chairman.
3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: The report isn’t a statistical survey, but paints a descriptive map of India’s satellite manufacturing supply chain.

🚀 Science, Tech & Environment Paragraph #27 of 30 (25 NOV)

📰 India’s satellite supply chain ‘highly dependent on imports’, says space body

📌 Published: 25 Nov 2026, 11:39:18 PM
🎙️ Desi Hinglish Voice Educator • 🚂 Live Train Line Highlight & Screen Lock

1. Core Context & Background: India’s space economy is currently valued at nearly $9 billion and is set to grow to $40-45 billion in less than a decade

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: India’s satellite supply chain is “highly dependent” on imports for critical components and the private sector’s contribution is limited to “structural assemblies” and “propulsion components” largely supplied by established public sector firms and vintage private firms, said a report by IN-SPACe, India’s regulatory-cum-promotional body for the private space sector. While pointing out the potential of India’s private space companies, the autonomous body under the Department of Space underlined the challenges ahead. Science Minister Jitendra Singh earlier this week said that India’s space economy is currently valued at nearly $9 billion and is set to increase to $40-45 billion in less than a decade, with the private sector set to grow from a a few startups “to nearly 400-500 companies in just a few years”. The Supply Chain Landscape of Satellite Manufacturing in India report, which was made public on Wednesday, says that nearly 60% of satellite costs were attributed to electronic, electrical and electromechanical components, and specialised materials, many of which are imported. India also has limited testing and certification facilities, which weakened prospects for acceptance in global markets. Many companies largely operated on a “project-based manufacturing model”, which disincentivised long-term investment in automation and production capacity, the report noted. Critical components often took a long time to procure – frequently 12-16 months – which led to project delays and hobbled responsiveness to market opportunities. There was also a shortage of trained and skilled personnel in satellite systems engineering, quality assurance, testing and qualification, besides limited private-sector research and development and technology transfer. The report was prepared by Brijesh Kumar Sol and Yudhishthir J. of IN-SPACe and “approved” by Pawan Goenka, IN-SPACe chairman.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: The report isn’t a statistical survey, but paints a descriptive map of India’s satellite manufacturing supply chain.

✓ Syn: Significant, Substantial, Strategic  |  ✖ Ant: Insignificant, Negligible, Trivial

महत्वपूर्ण विश्लेषणात्मक शब्द — इस लेख में 'Qualification' मुख्य प्रभाव और नीतिगत स्थिति को स्पष्ट करता है।
✓ Syn: Significant, Substantial, Strategic  |  ✖ Ant: Insignificant, Negligible, Trivial

Q1. Based on a critical reading of the above 🚀 Science, Tech & Environment passage on "India’s satellite supply chain ‘highly dependent on imports’, says space body", which of the following statements accurately reflects the central analytical observation of the text?
A. India’s space economy is currently valued at nearly $9 billion and is set to grow to $40-45 billion in less than a decade.
B. Contrary to the passage, the issue of 'India’s satellite supply chain ‘highly dependent' requires zero institutional or regulatory intervention at any level.
C. The passage argues that all empirical data and statutory mechanisms related to 'India’s satellite supply chain ‘highly depend' should be permanently discontinued.
D. The author contends that 'India’s satellite supply chain ‘highly depend' has no bearing on public governance, economy, or citizen welfare.
✅ Correct Answer: Option (A) — Sahi Jawab Option (A) hai. Is passage ki mukhya line saaf batati hai: "India’s space economy is currently valued at nearly $9 billion and is set to grow to $40-45 billion in less than a decade."
Q2. Which of the following key analytical points or conclusions is explicitly highlighted by the author in the passage regarding "India’s satellite supply chain ‘highly dependent on imports’, says space body"?
A. Advocating complete policy paralysis and ignoring ground-level implementation challenges.
B. The report isn’t a statistical survey, but paints a descriptive map of India’s satellite manufacturing supply chain.
C. Dismissing constitutional accountability and relying solely on unverified short-term measures.
D. Recommending the immediate suspension of all regulatory and scientific assessments mentioned in the text.
✅ Correct Answer: Option (B) — Sahi Jawab Option (B) hai. Lekhak ne passage ke vishleshan mein is baat par zor diya hai: "The report isn’t a statistical survey, but paints a descriptive map of India’s satellite manufacturing supply chain."

articles.title: Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: 1. Core Context & Background: BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance. The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: political parties / Bharatiya Janata Party / Punjab / voting / Indian National Congress / General Elections 2024 / Shiromani Akali Dal / Aam Aadmi Party / agriculture / economy / welfare

✍️ Editorial & Opinion Paragraph #2 of 30 (25 NOV)

📰 Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab

📌 Published: 25 Nov 2026, 11:55:57 PM
🎙️ Desi Hinglish Voice Educator • 🚂 Live Train Line Highlight & Screen Lock

1. Core Context & Background: BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance. The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: political parties / Bharatiya Janata Party / Punjab / voting / Indian National Congress / General Elections 2024 / Shiromani Akali Dal / Aam Aadmi Party / agriculture / economy / welfare

संवैधानिक — देश के संविधान (Constitution) के दायरे और मौलिक अधिकारों के अनुरूप।

A. BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up.
B. Contrary to the passage, the issue of 'Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance ' requires zero institutional or regulatory intervention at any level.
C. The passage argues that all empirical data and statutory mechanisms related to 'Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP allian' should be permanently discontinued.
D. The author contends that 'Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP allian' has no bearing on public governance, economy, or citizen welfare.
✅ Correct Answer: Option (A) — Sahi Jawab Option (A) hai. Is passage ki mukhya line saaf batati hai: "BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up."

C. Dismissing constitutional accountability and relying solely on unverified short-term measures.
D. Recommending the immediate suspension of all regulatory and scientific assessments mentioned in the text.

articles.title: Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: 1. Core Context & Background: Developed nations must bear much of the cost of carbon emissions

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, with a whimper. The 190-odd countries that had convened for nearly 12 days — a close to 50-hour overshoot — failed to agree on an overarching political statement , called a cover text, that acts as a stepping stone to future, collective global action on climate change. Usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations ; the COP31 leadership, helmed by Türkiye and Australia, thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings. The headline sought was a global electrification target: 35% of global final energy consumption will come from electricity by 2035, in the hope that this would reduce direct fossil fuel emissions. Ultimately, the cover text failed to pass muster because the European Union objected to the text’s lack of any explicit mention of ‘fossil fuel,’ let alone its phase-out. The COP process is arduously protracted as even a single country’s objection can stall progress. Country-blocks outside the EU, such as coalitions of the least developed countries, island nations, some South American countries — reportedly 130 countries — were also insistent on fossil fuel language. While COP 31 made some progress on old pathways, such as the Just Transition agreement, it is perplexing that the delegations could not make progress on the other big prong of negotiations: climate finance. The increase in solar panel installations and the significant shift towards battery use in grid storage and transport did not come cheap: the cost of the land required for their installation, their intermittent nature of being dependent on weather, grid upgrades all carry costs. It is global markets, imperfectly connected, but connected, that have managed to bring it to this stage over decades. India and China, major fossil emitters, with large, still indigent populations, are also leaders in total clean energy installations. Therefore it stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming. Economic crises are a feature, and not a bug, of the interconnected financial system enveloping the world and there are, undeniably, challenges to diverting the necessary finance towards countries most vulnerable to climate change impact. However, it is no longer prudent to sweep this under the rug by scuttling experimental approaches — namely carbon capture — as inimical to the broader commitment to eschew fossil fuel. When the primary framework climate agreement was crafted three decades ago, nobody envisaged AI and the drain that data centres portended or the wars that would see the vociferous antagonists of coal immediately shore up their gas reserves. Without honest good-faith dialogue, the COP is at risk of being a sideshow: a mortal blow to multilateralism.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: climate change / Turkey / politics / Australia / electricity production and distribution / energy and resource / European Union / solar / India / China / carbon emissions / population / economy / carbon capture and sequestration / Artificial Intelligence / data management storage

✍️ Editorial & Opinion Paragraph #5 of 30 (24 NOV)

📰 Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit

📌 Published: 24 Nov 2026, 12:07:07 PM
🎙️ Desi Hinglish Voice Educator • 🚂 Live Train Line Highlight & Screen Lock

1. Core Context & Background: Developed nations must bear much of the cost of carbon emissions

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, with a whimper. The 190-odd countries that had convened for nearly 12 days — a close to 50-hour overshoot — failed to agree on an overarching political statement , called a cover text, that acts as a stepping stone to future, collective global action on climate change. Usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations ; the COP31 leadership, helmed by Türkiye and Australia, thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings. The headline sought was a global electrification target: 35% of global final energy consumption will come from electricity by 2035, in the hope that this would reduce direct fossil fuel emissions. Ultimately, the cover text failed to pass muster because the European Union objected to the text’s lack of any explicit mention of ‘fossil fuel,’ let alone its phase-out. The COP process is arduously protracted as even a single country’s objection can stall progress. Country-blocks outside the EU, such as coalitions of the least developed countries, island nations, some South American countries — reportedly 130 countries — were also insistent on fossil fuel language. While COP 31 made some progress on old pathways, such as the Just Transition agreement, it is perplexing that the delegations could not make progress on the other big prong of negotiations: climate finance. The increase in solar panel installations and the significant shift towards battery use in grid storage and transport did not come cheap: the cost of the land required for their installation, their intermittent nature of being dependent on weather, grid upgrades all carry costs. It is global markets, imperfectly connected, but connected, that have managed to bring it to this stage over decades. India and China, major fossil emitters, with large, still indigent populations, are also leaders in total clean energy installations. Therefore it stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming. Economic crises are a feature, and not a bug, of the interconnected financial system enveloping the world and there are, undeniably, challenges to diverting the necessary finance towards countries most vulnerable to climate change impact. However, it is no longer prudent to sweep this under the rug by scuttling experimental approaches — namely carbon capture — as inimical to the broader commitment to eschew fossil fuel. When the primary framework climate agreement was crafted three decades ago, nobody envisaged AI and the drain that data centres portended or the wars that would see the vociferous antagonists of coal immediately shore up their gas reserves. Without honest good-faith dialogue, the COP is at risk of being a sideshow: a mortal blow to multilateralism.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: climate change / Turkey / politics / Australia / electricity production and distribution / energy and resource / European Union / solar / India / China / carbon emissions / population / economy / carbon capture and sequestration / Artificial Intelligence / data management storage

📚 TOP 4 HARD VOCABULARY WORDS EXTRACTED FROM THIS PARAGRAPH (TAP CARD FOR PICTURE & SYNONYMS):
Multilateral (Adjective)
बहुपक्षीय — जिसमें दो से अधिक देश (जैसे UN, G20, BRICS) मिलकर साझा फैसला लेते हैं।
✓ Syn: Plurilateral, International, Coalition-based  |  ✖ Ant: Unilateral, One-sided, Isolated
Indigenous (Adjective)
स्वदेशी — अपने ही देश (भारत) के वैज्ञानिकों और इंजीनियरों द्वारा देश में विकसित किया गया।
✓ Syn: Domestic, Home-grown, Native  |  ✖ Ant: Imported, Foreign, Exotic
Electrification (Noun)
महत्वपूर्ण विश्लेषणात्मक शब्द — इस लेख में 'Electrification' मुख्य प्रभाव और नीतिगत स्थिति को स्पष्ट करता है।
✓ Syn: Significant, Substantial, Strategic  |  ✖ Ant: Insignificant, Negligible, Trivial
Sequestration (Noun)
महत्वपूर्ण विश्लेषणात्मक शब्द — इस लेख में 'Sequestration' मुख्य प्रभाव और नीतिगत स्थिति को स्पष्ट करता है।
✓ Syn: Significant, Substantial, Strategic  |  ✖ Ant: Insignificant, Negligible, Trivial

Q1. Based on a critical reading of the above ✍️ Editorial & Opinion passage on "Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit", which of the following statements accurately reflects the central analytical observation of the text?
A. Developed nations must bear much of the cost of carbon emissions.
B. Contrary to the passage, the issue of 'Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit' requires zero institutional or regulatory intervention at any level.
C. The passage argues that all empirical data and statutory mechanisms related to 'Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit' should be permanently discontinued.
D. The author contends that 'Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit' has no bearing on public governance, economy, or citizen welfare.
✅ Correct Answer: Option (A) — Sahi Jawab Option (A) hai. Is passage ki mukhya line saaf batati hai: "Developed nations must bear much of the cost of carbon emissions."
Q2. Which of the following key analytical points or conclusions is explicitly highlighted by the author in the passage regarding "Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit"?
A. Advocating complete policy paralysis and ignoring ground-level implementation challenges.
B. climate change / Turkey / politics / Australia / electricity production and distribution / energy and resource / European Union / solar / India /...
C. Dismissing constitutional accountability and relying solely on unverified short-term measures.
D. Recommending the immediate suspension of all regulatory and scientific assessments mentioned in the text.

articles.title: Just verdict: on Myanmar and the International Court of Justice
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: 1. Core Context & Background: Rohingya cannot return unless Myanmar turns democratic

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: On November 19, the International Court of Justice held that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is for the first time that the court has found any state responsible for the crime. The verdict, with nine votes to six, was not lightly reached. Genocide requires proof of an intent to destroy a group. In the absence of direct evidence of a plan, the court could infer that intent only if it was “the only reasonable inference” from the facts, a high bar to affix responsibility. The facts it accepted are harrowing. In 2017, in what Myanmar’s army called “clearance operations” against the insurgent Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, 1,834 raped and 392 villages destroyed in northern Rakhine State. Over 7,00,000 fled to Bangladesh. Then Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, now Myanmar’s “civilian” President, called the “Bengali problem” an “unfinished job”. Myanmar argued that it had only been fighting insurgents or at worst, driving the Rohingya out or punishing them. The court said that the army drew no distinction between fighters and civilians, had no plan to move anyone, fired on fleeing people and killed children on a scale that could not be explained as punishment. Seen alongside decades of discrimination, the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy. The incidents of 2017 were no aberration. The army drove lakhs of Rohingya into Bangladesh in 1978 and 1991-92. The junta stripped the Rohingya of citizenship in 1982 and the state branded them as “foreigners” in Arakan, disenfranchising them in 2015. While the junta’s Bamar-Buddhist vision has oppressed every minority, the Rohingya have been subjected to the most brutality. More than 1.2 million are in Bangladesh, living in dilapidated conditions, made worse due to diminished international aid. The court ordered Myanmar to allow their safe, voluntary and dignified return and to compensate them, but it has no means of enforcing its judgment. Only the UN Security Council can, but it will be subject to vetoes by Myanmar’s backers, China and Russia. On the very day of the verdict, the two joined the U.S. in Shenzhen to declare the “immunities of State officials” of “paramount importance”. Others, India among them, have courted the regime in Naypyitaw regardless, following sham elections that made the junta leader civilian President earlier this year. And Rakhine State, mired in civil war, is now mostly held by the Arakan Army which is accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. Only a truly democratic, federal, plural and peaceful Myanmar can bring the Rohingya home in safety.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: international court or tribunal / Myanmar / Rohingya crisis / crime / armed Forces / sexual assault / Bangladesh / Citizenship / welfare / United Nations / China / Russia / India / democracy

✍️ Editorial & Opinion Paragraph #6 of 30 (24 NOV)

📰 Just verdict: on Myanmar and the International Court of Justice

📌 Published: 24 Nov 2026, 12:04:37 PM
🎙️ Desi Hinglish Voice Educator • 🚂 Live Train Line Highlight & Screen Lock

1. Core Context & Background: Rohingya cannot return unless Myanmar turns democratic

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: On November 19, the International Court of Justice held that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is for the first time that the court has found any state responsible for the crime. The verdict, with nine votes to six, was not lightly reached. Genocide requires proof of an intent to destroy a group. In the absence of direct evidence of a plan, the court could infer that intent only if it was “the only reasonable inference” from the facts, a high bar to affix responsibility. The facts it accepted are harrowing. In 2017, in what Myanmar’s army called “clearance operations” against the insurgent Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, 1,834 raped and 392 villages destroyed in northern Rakhine State. Over 7,00,000 fled to Bangladesh. Then Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, now Myanmar’s “civilian” President, called the “Bengali problem” an “unfinished job”. Myanmar argued that it had only been fighting insurgents or at worst, driving the Rohingya out or punishing them. The court said that the army drew no distinction between fighters and civilians, had no plan to move anyone, fired on fleeing people and killed children on a scale that could not be explained as punishment. Seen alongside decades of discrimination, the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy. The incidents of 2017 were no aberration. The army drove lakhs of Rohingya into Bangladesh in 1978 and 1991-92. The junta stripped the Rohingya of citizenship in 1982 and the state branded them as “foreigners” in Arakan, disenfranchising them in 2015. While the junta’s Bamar-Buddhist vision has oppressed every minority, the Rohingya have been subjected to the most brutality. More than 1.2 million are in Bangladesh, living in dilapidated conditions, made worse due to diminished international aid. The court ordered Myanmar to allow their safe, voluntary and dignified return and to compensate them, but it has no means of enforcing its judgment. Only the UN Security Council can, but it will be subject to vetoes by Myanmar’s backers, China and Russia. On the very day of the verdict, the two joined the U.S. in Shenzhen to declare the “immunities of State officials” of “paramount importance”. Others, India among them, have courted the regime in Naypyitaw regardless, following sham elections that made the junta leader civilian President earlier this year. And Rakhine State, mired in civil war, is now mostly held by the Arakan Army which is accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. Only a truly democratic, federal, plural and peaceful Myanmar can bring the Rohingya home in safety.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: international court or tribunal / Myanmar / Rohingya crisis / crime / armed Forces / sexual assault / Bangladesh / Citizenship / welfare / United Nations / China / Russia / India / democracy

In 2017, in what Myanmar’s army called “clearance operations” against the insurgent Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, 1,834 raped and 392 villages destroyed in northern Rakhine State. Over 7,00,000 fled to Bangladesh. Then Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, now Myanmar’s “civilian” President, called the “Bengali problem” an “unfinished job”. Myanmar argued that it had only been fighting insurgents or at worst, driving the Rohingya out or punishing them. The court said that the army drew no distinction between fighters and civilians, had no plan to move anyone, fired on fleeing people and killed children on a scale that could not be explained as punishment. Seen alongside decades of discrimination, the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy. The incidents of 2017 were no aberration. The army drove lakhs of Rohingya into Bangladesh in 1978 and 1991-92. The junta stripped the Rohingya of citizenship in 1982 and the state branded them as “foreigners” in Arakan, disenfranchising them in 2015. While the junta’s Bamar-Buddhist vision has oppressed every minority, the Rohingya have been subjected to the most brutality. More than 1.2 million are in Bangladesh, living in dilapidated conditions, made worse due to diminished international aid. The court ordered Myanmar to allow their safe, voluntary and dignified return and to compensate them, but it has no means of enforcing its judgment. Only the UN Security Council can, but it will be subject to vetoes by Myanmar’s backers, China and Russia. On the very day of the verdict, the two joined the U.S. in Shenzhen to declare the “immunities of State officials” of “paramount importance”. Others, India among them, have courted the regime in Naypyitaw regardless, following sham elections that made the junta leader civilian President earlier this year. And Rakhine State, mired in civil war, is now mostly held by the Arakan Army which is accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. Only a truly democratic, federal, plural and peaceful Myanmar can bring the Rohingya home in safety.

articles.title: Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: 1. Core Context & Background: India can no longer afford its silence on the multi-trillion dollar AI arms race

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The Initial Public Offering (IPO) of Anthropic , PBC is a mile marker in the arms race to develop superintelligent systems driven by generative AI . Traders valued the firm at $1.27 trillion, a denomination that is bound to become more and more familiar in an industry backed by an endless appetite for capital and unprecedented forms of financialisation. Anthropic’s statements emphasise warnings on the safety of its systems and the consequences of unbridled development of advanced systems. In the history of the development of this technology, this PR spin may just be a blip. After all, their testing has led to AI agents that have broken out of sandboxes and infected unsuspecting organisations’ internal systems: a deluge of agentic chaos that is already a reality has led to little signs of the firm backing its words with action. A familiar trend is playing out, with open source LLMs showing frontier capabilities that can back their erratic impulses, appearing in the space of just months, or sometimes weeks. Advocates of pacing the frontier and managing these emerging risks have been marginalised in a way that has little precedent in this century. It is time for governments to get involved, and specifically, for India to raise its voice on these risks, loudly and unequivocally.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: While India’s AI industry is nascent, its positions on international forums carry the weight of a sixth of humanity. A mix of cynical calculations and practical considerations have blunted the use of that voice, for example in the U.S.’s hugely destabilising war of choice against Iran, and Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza. In taking a strong position on what could be the defining transformation of this decade, India has little to lose, and a lot to contribute. India’s AI policies are geared towards diffusion and research of helpful capabilities that can trickle down to the common citizen. The capabilities that the Union government and State governments seek to boost by leveraging AI are removed from the frontier research wreaking havoc within the information security profession around the world. Out-of-control AI agents promise, moreover, significant disruption to outdated government and private systems online. While India has little commercial leverage to curb San Francisco’s accelerationism, its voice is sure to be noticed. India’s focus on AI in international fora, such as the AI Impact Summit in Delhi, has been on consensus. This approach must change. India cannot be silent amid a U.S.-China technological race which could lead to catastrophic damage. New Delhi must not allow the U.S. to stop it from pushing for AI safety.

✍️ Editorial & Opinion Paragraph #5 of 30 (24 NOV)

📰 Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO

📌 Published: 24 Nov 2026, 11:31:29 PM IST
🎙️ Desi Hinglish Voice Educator • 🚂 Live Train Line Highlight & Screen Lock

1. Core Context & Background: India can no longer afford its silence on the multi-trillion dollar AI arms race

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The Initial Public Offering (IPO) of Anthropic , PBC is a mile marker in the arms race to develop superintelligent systems driven by generative AI . Traders valued the firm at $1.27 trillion, a denomination that is bound to become more and more familiar in an industry backed by an endless appetite for capital and unprecedented forms of financialisation. Anthropic’s statements emphasise warnings on the safety of its systems and the consequences of unbridled development of advanced systems. In the history of the development of this technology, this PR spin may just be a blip. After all, their testing has led to AI agents that have broken out of sandboxes and infected unsuspecting organisations’ internal systems: a deluge of agentic chaos that is already a reality has led to little signs of the firm backing its words with action. A familiar trend is playing out, with open source LLMs showing frontier capabilities that can back their erratic impulses, appearing in the space of just months, or sometimes weeks. Advocates of pacing the frontier and managing these emerging risks have been marginalised in a way that has little precedent in this century. It is time for governments to get involved, and specifically, for India to raise its voice on these risks, loudly and unequivocally.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: While India’s AI industry is nascent, its positions on international forums carry the weight of a sixth of humanity. A mix of cynical calculations and practical considerations have blunted the use of that voice, for example in the U.S.’s hugely destabilising war of choice against Iran, and Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza. In taking a strong position on what could be the defining transformation of this decade, India has little to lose, and a lot to contribute. India’s AI policies are geared towards diffusion and research of helpful capabilities that can trickle down to the common citizen. The capabilities that the Union government and State governments seek to boost by leveraging AI are removed from the frontier research wreaking havoc within the information security profession around the world. Out-of-control AI agents promise, moreover, significant disruption to outdated government and private systems online. While India has little commercial leverage to curb San Francisco’s accelerationism, its voice is sure to be noticed. India’s focus on AI in international fora, such as the AI Impact Summit in Delhi, has been on consensus. This approach must change. India cannot be silent amid a U.S.-China technological race which could lead to catastrophic damage. New Delhi must not allow the U.S. to stop it from pushing for AI safety.

📚 TOP 4 HARD VOCABULARY WORDS EXTRACTED FROM THIS PARAGRAPH (TAP CARD FOR PICTURE & SYNONYMS):
Financialisation (Noun)
वित्तीयकरण — इस अनुच्छेद में 'Financialisation' का प्रयोग एक महत्वपूर्ण प्रशासनिक और विश्लेषणात्मक अर्थ में किया गया है।
✓ Syn: Significant, Substantial, Strategic  |  ✖ Ant: Insignificant, Negligible, Trivial
Transformation (Noun)
परिवर्तन — इस अनुच्छेद में 'Transformation' का प्रयोग एक महत्वपूर्ण प्रशासनिक और विश्लेषणात्मक अर्थ में किया गया है।
✓ Syn: Significant, Substantial, Strategic  |  ✖ Ant: Insignificant, Negligible, Trivial
International (Adjective)
महत्वपूर्ण विश्लेषणात्मक शब्द — इस लेख में 'International' मुख्य प्रभाव और नीतिगत स्थिति को स्पष्ट करता है।
✓ Syn: Comprehensive, Influential, Decisive  |  ✖ Ant: Superficial, Ineffective, Fragile
Technological (Adjective)
महत्वपूर्ण विश्लेषणात्मक शब्द — इस लेख में 'Technological' मुख्य प्रभाव और नीतिगत स्थिति को स्पष्ट करता है।
✓ Syn: Comprehensive, Influential, Decisive  |  ✖ Ant: Superficial, Ineffective, Fragile
🧠 2 ANALYTICAL EXAM QUESTIONS BASED ON THIS EDITORIAL:
Q1. Based on a critical reading of the above ✍️ Editorial & Opinion passage on "Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO", which of the following statements accurately reflects the central analytical observation of the text?
A. India can no longer afford its silence on the multi-trillion dollar AI arms race.
B. Contrary to the passage, the issue of 'Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO' requires zero institutional or regulatory intervention at any level.
C. The passage argues that all empirical data and statutory mechanisms related to 'Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO' should be permanently discontinued.
D. The author contends that 'Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO' has no bearing on public governance, economy, or citizen welfare.
✅ Correct Answer: Option (A) — Sahi Jawab Option (A) hai. Is passage ki mukhya line saaf batati hai: "India can no longer afford its silence on the multi-trillion dollar AI arms race." (Hinglish Arth: भारत अब खरबों डॉलर की एआई हथियारों की होड़ पर अपनी चुप्पी बर्दाश्त नहीं कर सकता)
Q2. Which of the following key analytical points or conclusions is explicitly highlighted by the author in the passage regarding "Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO"?
A. Advocating complete policy paralysis and ignoring ground-level implementation challenges.
B. to stop it from pushing for AI safety.
C. Dismissing constitutional accountability and relying solely on unverified short-term measures.
D. Recommending the immediate suspension of all regulatory and scientific assessments mentioned in the text.
✅ Correct Answer: Option (B) — Sahi Jawab Option (B) hai. Lekhak ne passage ke vishleshan mein is baat par zor diya hai: "to stop it from pushing for AI safety." (Hinglish Arth: इसे एआई सुरक्षा पर जोर देने से रोकने के लिए।)

articles.title: Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilateral summit
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: 1. Core Context & Background: U.S., China, Russia must draw up a roadmap for talks on nuclear weapons

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The first trilateral summit between the Presidents of China, the U.S. and Russia , held in Shenzhen on November 19, reflected both the changing global order and the leaders’ shared desire to remain engaged with one another in an increasingly unpredictable world. For U.S. President Donald Trump, the summit was a platform where he could push for joint talks between the world’s three largest nuclear powers on reducing nuclear warheads. After the New START treaty between the U.S. and Russia expired in February 2026, Moscow had signalled that it was ready for talks, but Mr. Trump wanted to involve China as well. For President Xi Jinping, the summit reinforced China’s position as a peer competitor to the U.S. While Russia seeks to deepen partnership with China, the U.S. is looking to build strategic stability. And for Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom the West sought to isolate after he launched the invasion of Ukraine, the summit offered a seat at the high table. The decision to start trilateral talks on nuclear arms and the joint declaration, which stated that ‘a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought’, are steps in the right direction. But much will depend on what follows.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Many had compared the meet to the 1945 Yalta Conference, when Russian leader Joseph Stalin, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill met to discuss the future of post-War Europe. But Shenzhen was not a summit of the victors of a major war. This was more about three great powers setting terms of engagement in a changing world. The summit failed to achieve any breakthrough on any of the issues on the agenda — nuclear arms reduction, non-proliferation or the Ukraine war — or even offer a road map for the future. Moreover, it is not clear if the Shenzhen spirit could be sustained in the medium to long-term as another President in the U.S. could take a very different approach towards Russia and China. The three leaders have called for reform of the UN. While it is a welcome move, any attempt to reform the international system and institutions must also involve other powers, particularly rising middle powers such as India, South Africa and Brazil. But the Shenzhen framework could bring greater stability and predictability to great-power relations. This is important given that two of the Big Three are currently waging two separate wars. The leaders should draw up a clear road map for nuclear talks and other key issues outlined in the Shenzhen declaration, with realistic and achievable objectives. Otherwise, the summit would amount to little more than another diplomatic photo-op.

✍️ Editorial & Opinion Paragraph #6 of 30 (24 NOV)

📰 Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilateral summit

📌 Published: 24 Nov 2026, 11:31:29 PM IST
🎙️ Desi Hinglish Voice Educator • 🚂 Live Train Line Highlight & Screen Lock

1. Core Context & Background: U.S., China, Russia must draw up a roadmap for talks on nuclear weapons

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The first trilateral summit between the Presidents of China, the U.S. and Russia , held in Shenzhen on November 19, reflected both the changing global order and the leaders’ shared desire to remain engaged with one another in an increasingly unpredictable world. For U.S. President Donald Trump, the summit was a platform where he could push for joint talks between the world’s three largest nuclear powers on reducing nuclear warheads. After the New START treaty between the U.S. and Russia expired in February 2026, Moscow had signalled that it was ready for talks, but Mr. Trump wanted to involve China as well. For President Xi Jinping, the summit reinforced China’s position as a peer competitor to the U.S. While Russia seeks to deepen partnership with China, the U.S. is looking to build strategic stability. And for Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom the West sought to isolate after he launched the invasion of Ukraine, the summit offered a seat at the high table. The decision to start trilateral talks on nuclear arms and the joint declaration, which stated that ‘a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought’, are steps in the right direction. But much will depend on what follows.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Many had compared the meet to the 1945 Yalta Conference, when Russian leader Joseph Stalin, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill met to discuss the future of post-War Europe. But Shenzhen was not a summit of the victors of a major war. This was more about three great powers setting terms of engagement in a changing world. The summit failed to achieve any breakthrough on any of the issues on the agenda — nuclear arms reduction, non-proliferation or the Ukraine war — or even offer a road map for the future. Moreover, it is not clear if the Shenzhen spirit could be sustained in the medium to long-term as another President in the U.S. could take a very different approach towards Russia and China. The three leaders have called for reform of the UN. While it is a welcome move, any attempt to reform the international system and institutions must also involve other powers, particularly rising middle powers such as India, South Africa and Brazil. But the Shenzhen framework could bring greater stability and predictability to great-power relations. This is important given that two of the Big Three are currently waging two separate wars. The leaders should draw up a clear road map for nuclear talks and other key issues outlined in the Shenzhen declaration, with realistic and achievable objectives. Otherwise, the summit would amount to little more than another diplomatic photo-op.

📚 TOP 4 HARD VOCABULARY WORDS EXTRACTED FROM THIS PARAGRAPH (TAP CARD FOR PICTURE & SYNONYMS):
Predictably (Adverb)
जैसा पहले से अनुमान था — बिना किसी आश्चर्य के बिल्कुल पूर्वानुमान के मुताबिक होना।
✓ Syn: Foreseeably, Expectedly, Inevitably  |  ✖ Ant: Unexpectedly, Surprisingly, Abruptly
Institutional (Adjective)
संस्थागत — देश की संवैधानिक या सरकारी संस्थाओं के नियमों और ढांचे से जुड़ा हुआ।
✓ Syn: Systemic, Organizational, Constitutional  |  ✖ Ant: Individual, Informal, Unorganized
Sustainability (Noun)
सतत विकास — पर्यावरण और भविष्य की पीढ़ियों को नुकसान पहुँचाए बिना लंबे समय तक चलने वाला विकास।
✓ Syn: Viability, Eco-balance, Durability  |  ✖ Ant: Depletion, Unsustainability, Destruction
Proliferation (Noun)
प्रसार — इस अनुच्छेद में 'Proliferation' का प्रयोग एक महत्वपूर्ण प्रशासनिक और विश्लेषणात्मक अर्थ में किया गया है।
✓ Syn: Significant, Substantial, Strategic  |  ✖ Ant: Insignificant, Negligible, Trivial
🧠 2 ANALYTICAL EXAM QUESTIONS BASED ON THIS EDITORIAL:
Q1. Based on a critical reading of the above ✍️ Editorial & Opinion passage on "Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilateral summit", which of the following statements accurately reflects the central analytical observation of the text?
A. U.S., China, Russia must draw up a roadmap for talks on nuclear weapons.
B. Contrary to the passage, the issue of 'Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilateral s' requires zero institutional or regulatory intervention at any level.
C. The passage argues that all empirical data and statutory mechanisms related to 'Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilatera' should be permanently discontinued.
D. The author contends that 'Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilatera' has no bearing on public governance, economy, or citizen welfare.
✅ Correct Answer: Option (A) — Sahi Jawab Option (A) hai. Is passage ki mukhya line saaf batati hai: "U.S., China, Russia must draw up a roadmap for talks on nuclear weapons." (Hinglish Arth: अमेरिका, चीन, रूस को परमाणु हथियारों पर बातचीत के लिए एक रोडमैप तैयार करना चाहिए)
Q2. Which of the following key analytical points or conclusions is explicitly highlighted by the author in the passage regarding "Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilateral summit"?
A. Advocating complete policy paralysis and ignoring ground-level implementation challenges.
B. Otherwise, the summit would amount to little more than another diplomatic photo-op.
C. Dismissing constitutional accountability and relying solely on unverified short-term measures.
D. Recommending the immediate suspension of all regulatory and scientific assessments mentioned in the text.
✅ Correct Answer: Option (B) — Sahi Jawab Option (B) hai. Lekhak ne passage ke vishleshan mein is baat par zor diya hai: "Otherwise, the summit would amount to little more than another diplomatic photo-op." (Hinglish Arth: अन्यथा, शिखर सम्मेलन एक और राजनयिक फोटो-ऑप से थोड़ा अधिक होगा।)

For President Xi Jinping, the summit reinforced China’s position as a peer competitor to the U.S. While Russia seeks to deepen partnership with China, the U.S. is looking to build strategic stability. And for Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom the West sought to isolate after he launched the invasion of Ukraine, the summit offered a seat at the high table. The decision to start trilateral talks on nuclear arms and the joint declaration, which stated that ‘a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought’, are steps in the right direction. But much will depend on what follows.
• 3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Many had compared the meet to the 1945 Yalta Conference, when Russian leader Joseph Stalin, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill met to discuss the future of post-War Europe. But Shenzhen was not a summit of the victors of a major war. This was more about three great powers setting terms of engagement in a changing world. The summit failed to achieve any breakthrough on any of the issues on the agenda — nuclear arms reduction, non-proliferation or the Ukraine war — or even offer a road map for the future. Moreover, it is not clear if the Shenzhen spirit could be sustained in the medium to long-term as another President in the U.S. could take a very different approach towards Russia and China. The three leaders have called for reform of the UN. While it is a welcome move, any attempt to reform the international system and institutions must also involve other powers, particularly rising middle powers such as India, South Africa and Brazil. But the Shenzhen framework could bring greater stability and predictability to great-power relations. This is important given that two of the Big Three are currently waging two separate wars. The leaders should draw up a clear road map for nuclear talks and other key issues outlined in the Shenzhen declaration, with realistic and achievable objectives. Otherwise, the summit would amount to little more than another diplomatic photo-op.

Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convener Saurav Das on Monday (November 23, 2026) alleged that he was stopped from travelling to the U.K. to attend an event at the University of Oxford, where he was invited to speak on the "cockroach movement". In posts on X, Mr. Das said he was stopped at the immigration counter at the Delhi airport before boarding his 1 a.m. flight to London. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke alleged that someone in power was jealous of Mr. Das receiving an invitation from the University of Oxford. Mr. Das said, "I have been stopped by this cowardly Modi Govt at the Delhi Airport from flying to London to deliver a lecture at the University of Oxford." "This coward government did not allow me to board my flight to London where I was invited by prestigious universities like Oxford, Cambridge, LSE, Edinburgh to deliver talks on the cockroach movement. "Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual govt was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions!" he said. Mr. Das said he has been invited by the Oxford University Students' Union for a panel discussion. "And that's why I was going to London. But as soon as I went to the immigration check, I came to know that my passport has been flagged," he said. "Why is the government so scared of an educated youth going among educated people and having an intellectual discussion?
3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: "I wish I was Nirav Modi. I wish I was Vijay Mallya. I wish I had looted thousands of crores from the banks..." he said.

articles.title: The Bilkis Bano order — justice deferred again
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: 1. Core Context & Background: The right to liberty cannot undermine a survivor’s dignity, voice and difficult quest for justice

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: “Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought,” said John Rawls in A Theory of Justice. The American political philosopher’s line is easy to admire yet hard to practice. When an institution cannot be trusted to hear a wronged person, the old maxim justice delayed is justice denied begins to sound less like a warning than a description. For nearly a quarter of a century, Bilkis Bano, a survivor of the 2002 Gujarat riots who was gang-raped by 11 men while pregnant and lost some members of her family, has had to prove over and over again what happened to her was real, that it was a crime, and that the law should answer it. Each time, she has done so with a defiant courage that has become a testament to the Republic’s conscience. She now may have to do it again. On October 28, 2026, a Supreme Court Bench of Justices M.M. Sundresh and Prasanna B. Varale suspended the life sentences of two of the 11 men convicted of gang-raping her and murdering some members of her family, granting them bail pending their appeals. Ms. Bano told the media that she learnt of the order just a few days ago through the press. The counsel for the two men later issued a statement on November 21, rejecting Ms. Bano’s allegation that she was kept in the dark about the proceedings but asserting that she was not party even in High Court. “It is still baffling to me that for the second time after this order was passed, I have not been summoned to appear before the Supreme Court, nor has anything been heard from me,” Ms. Bano said in a statement through her attorneys. It is a sentence that no citizen, for whatever reason he may have for taking the oath regardless of his opinion of the merits of the order, should find easy to read. Every word counts here. This case is designed to elicit both outrage and defensive responses. No one is found “not guilty” in the order. The principles, which were upheld by the Bombay High Court in 2017, remain the same. What the Bench has done is that it has merely suspended the sentences of the two men, Bipinchand Kanhaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya, until their appeals are disposed of, by pointing out that both men have been in jail for over 17 years, one of them has a severe disability, and their appeals raise questions of fact and law that require examination. The Additional Solicitor General opposed the pleas. The convicts’ appeals against the High Court’s judgment are still to be decided. There is no objection to the order in the context of not subscribing to retributive or deterrent theories of punishment. However, at a time when there is talk of making the criminal justice system victim-centric, why was victimology forgotten in this case? That is the central question which survives despite the November 23, 2026 order by the same Bench releasing Siraj Pada, one of the convicts of the Sabarmati Express coach fire on similar grounds.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Gujarat / riots / crime, law and justice / sexual assault / court / media / judiciary (system of justice) / prison / criminal / constitution / human rights / Mumbai / government

🏛️ Political, National & Polity Paragraph #8 of 30 (24 NOV)

📰 The Bilkis Bano order — justice deferred again

📌 Published: 24 Nov 2026, 01:15:52 AM
🎙️ Desi Hinglish Voice Educator • 🚂 Live Train Line Highlight & Screen Lock

1. Core Context & Background: The right to liberty cannot undermine a survivor’s dignity, voice and difficult quest for justice

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: “Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought,” said John Rawls in A Theory of Justice. The American political philosopher’s line is easy to admire yet hard to practice. When an institution cannot be trusted to hear a wronged person, the old maxim justice delayed is justice denied begins to sound less like a warning than a description. For nearly a quarter of a century, Bilkis Bano, a survivor of the 2002 Gujarat riots who was gang-raped by 11 men while pregnant and lost some members of her family, has had to prove over and over again what happened to her was real, that it was a crime, and that the law should answer it. Each time, she has done so with a defiant courage that has become a testament to the Republic’s conscience. She now may have to do it again. On October 28, 2026, a Supreme Court Bench of Justices M.M. Sundresh and Prasanna B. Varale suspended the life sentences of two of the 11 men convicted of gang-raping her and murdering some members of her family, granting them bail pending their appeals. Ms. Bano told the media that she learnt of the order just a few days ago through the press. The counsel for the two men later issued a statement on November 21, rejecting Ms. Bano’s allegation that she was kept in the dark about the proceedings but asserting that she was not party even in High Court. “It is still baffling to me that for the second time after this order was passed, I have not been summoned to appear before the Supreme Court, nor has anything been heard from me,” Ms. Bano said in a statement through her attorneys. It is a sentence that no citizen, for whatever reason he may have for taking the oath regardless of his opinion of the merits of the order, should find easy to read. Every word counts here. This case is designed to elicit both outrage and defensive responses. No one is found “not guilty” in the order. The principles, which were upheld by the Bombay High Court in 2017, remain the same. What the Bench has done is that it has merely suspended the sentences of the two men, Bipinchand Kanhaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya, until their appeals are disposed of, by pointing out that both men have been in jail for over 17 years, one of them has a severe disability, and their appeals raise questions of fact and law that require examination. The Additional Solicitor General opposed the pleas. The convicts’ appeals against the High Court’s judgment are still to be decided. There is no objection to the order in the context of not subscribing to retributive or deterrent theories of punishment. However, at a time when there is talk of making the criminal justice system victim-centric, why was victimology forgotten in this case? That is the central question which survives despite the November 23, 2026 order by the same Bench releasing Siraj Pada, one of the convicts of the Sabarmati Express coach fire on similar grounds.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Gujarat / riots / crime, law and justice / sexual assault / court / media / judiciary (system of justice) / prison / criminal / constitution / human rights / Mumbai / government

📚 TOP 4 HARD VOCABULARY WORDS EXTRACTED FROM THIS PARAGRAPH (TAP CARD FOR PICTURE & SYNONYMS):
Institutional (Adjective)
संस्थागत — देश की संवैधानिक या सरकारी संस्थाओं के नियमों और ढांचे से जुड़ा हुआ।
✓ Syn: Systemic, Organizational, Constitutional  |  ✖ Ant: Individual, Informal, Unorganized
Constitutional (Adjective)
संवैधानिक — देश के संविधान (Constitution) के दायरे और मौलिक अधिकारों के अनुरूप।
✓ Syn: Statutory, Legitimate, Lawful  |  ✖ Ant: Unconstitutional, Illegal, Arbitrary
Description (Adjective / Verb)
विवरण — इस अनुच्छेद में 'Description' का प्रयोग एक महत्वपूर्ण प्रशासनिक और विश्लेषणात्मक अर्थ में किया गया है।
✓ Syn: Restrictive, Counteractive, Adverse  |  ✖ Ant: Constructive, Supportive, Favorable
Kanhaiyalal (Adjective)
-कन्हैयालाल — इस अनुच्छेद में 'Kanhaiyalal' का प्रयोग एक महत्वपूर्ण प्रशासनिक और विश्लेषणात्मक अर्थ में किया गया है।
✓ Syn: Comprehensive, Influential, Decisive  |  ✖ Ant: Superficial, Ineffective, Fragile
🧠 2 ANALYTICAL EXAM QUESTIONS BASED ON THIS EDITORIAL:
Q1. Based on a critical reading of the above 🏛️ Political, National & Polity passage on "The Bilkis Bano order — justice deferred again", which of the following statements accurately reflects the central analytical observation of the text?
A. The right to liberty cannot undermine a survivor’s dignity, voice and difficult quest for justice.
B. Contrary to the passage, the issue of 'The Bilkis Bano order — justice deferred again' requires zero institutional or regulatory intervention at any level.
C. The passage argues that all empirical data and statutory mechanisms related to 'The Bilkis Bano order — justice deferred agai' should be permanently discontinued.
D. The author contends that 'The Bilkis Bano order — justice deferred agai' has no bearing on public governance, economy, or citizen welfare.
✅ Correct Answer: Option (A) — Sahi Jawab Option (A) hai. Is passage ki mukhya line saaf batati hai: "The right to liberty cannot undermine a survivor’s dignity, voice and difficult quest for justice." (Hinglish Arth: स्वतंत्रता का अधिकार किसी उत्तरजीवी की गरिमा, आवाज़ और न्याय की कठिन खोज को कमज़ोर नहीं कर सकता)
Q2. Which of the following key analytical points or conclusions is explicitly highlighted by the author in the passage regarding "The Bilkis Bano order — justice deferred again"?
A. Advocating complete policy paralysis and ignoring ground-level implementation challenges.
B. Gujarat / riots / crime, law and justice / sexual assault / court / media / judiciary (system of justice) / prison / criminal / constitution / human...
C. Dismissing constitutional accountability and relying solely on unverified short-term measures.
D. Recommending the immediate suspension of all regulatory and scientific assessments mentioned in the text.
✅ Correct Answer: Option (B) — Sahi Jawab Option (B) hai. Lekhak ne passage ke vishleshan mein is baat par zor diya hai: "Gujarat / riots / crime, law and justice / sexual assault / court / media / judiciary (system of justice) / prison / criminal / constitution / human..." articles.title: Power outage during Minister’s programme in Kannur: KSEB staff rally behind suspended sub-engineer
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: 1. Core Context & Background: Employees of the Kerala State Electricity Board (KSEB), under the banner of a joint action committee of officers and workers’ organisations, launched an agitation in Kannur on Monday (November 23) demanding the withdrawal of the suspension of sub-engineer Satheesh Babu in connection with a brief power disruption during a programme attended by Electricity Minister Sunny Joseph on Saturday (November 21).

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Hundreds of employees and officers from various KSEB offices joined the protest, with the organisations warning that the agitation would continue until the suspension was revoked. They also indicated that the protest could be extended across the State if the management failed to reconsider its decision. The employees said the power supply had been disrupted for only about nine minutes as part of urgent maintenance work after a potentially dangerous fault was detected in an 11 kV feeder supplying the Kannur town area. They maintained that the interruption was necessary to avert a possible accident and that the required information had been communicated to consumers in advance through the outage management system and WhatsApp groups. They alleged that neither the division office nor the section office had been informed about the Minister’s programme and that there was no question of deliberately disrupting the power supply. They also said that Mr. Babu had submitted an explanation when the authorities sought his response, but he was suspended without a proper preliminary inquiry. The controversy erupted after the power disruption during the Electricity Minister’s programme at Jawahar Library Hall in Kannur on November 21. MLA T.O. Mohanan, who was present at the event, lodged a complaint with the KSEB chairman alleging deliberate disruption of the power supply. The suspension followed the complaint. Inaugurating the protest in front of the KSEB office in Kannur, MLA K.V. Sumesh described the suspension as arbitrary, undemocratic and an insult to the dignity of the employees. He demanded its immediate withdrawal and warned that failure to do so would lead to a strong public agitation across the State. He questioned the rationale behind suspecting an employee of deliberately disrupting power supply for political reasons, irrespective of which political front was in power.
3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: “Employees could not be expected to compromise safety procedures because a Minister or an elected representative was attending a programme,” he said.

🏛️ Political, National & Polity Paragraph #9 of 30 (24 NOV)

📰 Power outage during Minister’s programme in Kannur: KSEB staff rally behind suspended sub-engineer

📌 Published: 24 Nov 2026, 01:15:31 AM
🎙️ Desi Hinglish Voice Educator • 🚂 Live Train Line Highlight & Screen Lock

1. Core Context & Background: Employees of the Kerala State Electricity Board (KSEB), under the banner of a joint action committee of officers and workers’ organisations, launched an agitation in Kannur on Monday (November 23) demanding the withdrawal of the suspension of sub-engineer Satheesh Babu in connection with a brief power disruption during a programme attended by Electricity Minister Sunny Joseph on Saturday (November 21).

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Hundreds of employees and officers from various KSEB offices joined the protest, with the organisations warning that the agitation would continue until the suspension was revoked. They also indicated that the protest could be extended across the State if the management failed to reconsider its decision. The employees said the power supply had been disrupted for only about nine minutes as part of urgent maintenance work after a potentially dangerous fault was detected in an 11 kV feeder supplying the Kannur town area. They maintained that the interruption was necessary to avert a possible accident and that the required information had been communicated to consumers in advance through the outage management system and WhatsApp groups. They alleged that neither the division office nor the section office had been informed about the Minister’s programme and that there was no question of deliberately disrupting the power supply. They also said that Mr. Babu had submitted an explanation when the authorities sought his response, but he was suspended without a proper preliminary inquiry. The controversy erupted after the power disruption during the Electricity Minister’s programme at Jawahar Library Hall in Kannur on November 21. MLA T.O. Mohanan, who was present at the event, lodged a complaint with the KSEB chairman alleging deliberate disruption of the power supply. The suspension followed the complaint. Inaugurating the protest in front of the KSEB office in Kannur, MLA K.V. Sumesh described the suspension as arbitrary, undemocratic and an insult to the dignity of the employees. He demanded its immediate withdrawal and warned that failure to do so would lead to a strong public agitation across the State. He questioned the rationale behind suspecting an employee of deliberately disrupting power supply for political reasons, irrespective of which political front was in power.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: “Employees could not be expected to compromise safety procedures because a Minister or an elected representative was attending a programme,” he said.
